← Ocean proof

Phone tuning round

Your first result: WebGPU runs, approximately 6 fps at 1170×2532 (reported by you). This version reduces the workload and fixes the wave clock. Its phone performance is awaiting your retest.

The current app has not been changed. No migration is approved or started.

What we can establish now

The ocean, breaker, spray, foam and water-material source is the pinned Tidewater implementation. There are no wave-shape formula substitutions. The host adds a spray ring-budget adapter; it changes active slots, dispatch and draw counts, not particle force formulas. The test host supplies DayBuoy's camera and beach geometry, and three explicitly labelled height inputs. The phone starts at DPR 1.25, dropping as low as 1.0. Automatic quality reduces mesh LOD, active spray slots, refraction resolution, environment reflection refresh and cloud-buffer resolution. Phone reflections use a 64² cube. Wave height, period, the FFT spectrum and curling-lip geometry are unchanged.

The updated iPhone benchmark and 10-second timing clip have not been run by this session. The page now records a timed clip with real and shader clocks on screen. Clock tests pass at 1/6/15/30/60/120 fps and across stalls. The added spray budget shader passed a Dawn null-backend compilation check; this is not a rendering test. This environment has no working WebGPU rendering adapter or access to an iPhone. Source hashes, import resolution, syntax, camera projection, clock invariance and automatic-quality checks passed. A Dawn null-backend pipeline attempt failed at Tidewater’s 18,432-byte workgroup requirement (that adapter exposes 16,384), followed by invalid-layout errors. It produced no pixels and is not a rendering pass. The page exposes its actual backend, measures on the device that opens it and provides recording/export controls where the browser supports them.

Two paths

PathWhat changes / risks
A · Translate ocean to WebGLRewrite WGSL shaders and compute-driven FFT, foam, swash and particle updates as WebGL-compatible passes. Rebuild buffer/binding and depth/refraction handling. Our current scene renderer can stay, but this is a large reimplementation with the greatest risk of losing the reference appearance. Phone performance is unknown.
B · Move scene rendering to WebGPUKeep Tidewater's connected ocean implementation. Adapt our beach geometry/material, sky/clouds, sun/moon display, shadows, effects and camera projection to the renderer. Existing HTML/CSS menu, forecast data, NOAA calculations and gesture logic can remain with an adapter. Risks: iPhone GPU limits, shader startup, thermal load and exact visual parity of our sky/sand. Devices without WebGPU need an explicit supported-device policy or separate legacy path.

B is the stronger fidelity path because it preserves the ocean implementation the reference demonstrates. That is a provisional engineering recommendation—not proof that it runs acceptably on an iPhone. Approve a migration only after reviewing the actual phone output and sustained frame times.

Safari 26 introduced WebGPU on iOS. Support alone does not establish this renderer's compatibility or speed. Official WebKit documentation.

A disappointing proof should first be traced to camera framing, scale, slope or device limits. It does not establish that every possible port would fail.

Important comparison limits

The requested 1 / 3 / 5 ft values are controlled test inputs, not claims about today's forecast. Tidewater's shore-wave parameter is amplitude in metres, so H/2 is used. Its offshore spectrum is scaled relatively; significant wave height has not been independently calibrated.

Our physical beach slope is 0.105. Tidewater's internal swash conversion still uses its original 0.066 nominal slope. Changing that would be a source adaptation, so it is disclosed here rather than hidden in an “unchanged” proof.

The two oceans share the camera, beach profile, sun direction and sea-state test inputs. They retain their respective materials and lighting. Default Tidewater sky/cloud rendering is present for its water reflections; this is not a proposed replacement for the app's sky.
